A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $V$ be a real or complex vector space with a norm $\|\cdot\|$. Then $\|\cdot\|$ is induced by an inner product on $V$ if and only if it satisfies the parallelogram law

$$\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2 \qquad (x,y\in V).$$

In that case the inner product is unique, and it is given by the real polarisation formula

$$\langle x,y\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2\bigr)$$

in the real case, and by the complex polarisation formula

$$\langle x,y\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2+i\|x+iy\|^2-i\|x-iy\|^2\bigr)$$

in the complex case with the first-variable-linear convention.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]),
with the root convention that
each inner product is linear in its first argument. Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for
the complex-linear endomorphisms of $H$ and $\mathcal L(H,K)$ for the
complex-linear maps from $H$ to $K$ ([[def-linear-map]]). A **finite Kraus
representation** of a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ is a finite family
$(K_a)_{a\in A}\subseteq\mathcal L(H,K)$ such that

$$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where $K_a^\dagger:K\to H$ is the adjoint
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]), which exists
uniquely in finite dimensions ([[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]).
The composition $K_a\circ X\circ K_a^\dagger$ maps $K$ to $K$, so the sum
defines an output endomorphism for each input endomorphism $X$. The index set
$A$ may be empty; its sum is then the zero map. Zero operators are allowed in
a nonempty family.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space. If $D:V\to V$ is linear
and $\operatorname{tr}(D\circ A)=0$ for every linear map $A:V\to V$, then $D=0$.
Equivalently, the trace pairing $(D,A)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(D\circ A)$
has the property that its only first input pairing to zero with every second
input is $D=0$. This includes the zero space.

**unitary conjugation map**
$$\operatorname{Ad}_U:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K),\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_U(X)=UXU^\dagger.$$

spaces ([[def-linear-map]]). It is well-defined because the composition is
$U\circ X\circ U^\dagger:K\to K$, and it is complex-linear in $X$.

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

complex inner-product spaces and let
$V:H\to K$ be a linear isometry. Then $V^\dagger V=I_H$. If $V$ is also
surjective, then $VV^\dagger=I_K$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}$ be finite-dimensional (have
finite bases by [[def-dimension]]) complex inner-product spaces
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), and fix an
ordered orthonormal basis $\mathcal B=(e_0,\ldots,e_{n-1})$ of
$H_{\mathrm{in}}$ (the register basis convention is in
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). For $i,j<n$, let
$E_{ij}\in\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})$ be the matrix unit, where
$\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})$ denotes the complex-linear endomorphisms
([[def-linear-map]]),
$E_{ij}x:=\langle x,e_j\rangle e_i$, using the root inner product convention
that the first argument is linear. Given a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}})\to\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{out}})$
([[def-linear-map]]), its **Choi matrix relative to $\mathcal B$** is

$$J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j<n} E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in\mathcal L(H_{\mathrm{in}}\otimes H_{\mathrm{out}}),$$
where the operator tensor is the tensor map of [[def-qc-tensor-map]] and the
tensor inner product is the finite product pairing in
[[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]].

The tensor factors are ordered input first and output second. The coordinate
matrix has size $(n\,\dim H_{\mathrm{out}})\times(n\,\dim H_{\mathrm{out}})$.
The chosen input basis is part of this definition. If the input basis is
empty, the displayed sum is empty; if $\dim H_{\mathrm{out}}=0$, each
summand is zero and $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ is the unique endomorphism of the
zero-dimensional tensor product.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]),
with the root convention that
each inner product is linear in its first argument. Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for
the complex-linear endomorphisms of $H$ and $\mathcal L(H,K)$ for the
complex-linear maps from $H$ to $K$ ([[def-linear-map]]). A **finite Kraus
representation** of a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ is a finite family
$(K_a)_{a\in A}\subseteq\mathcal L(H,K)$ such that

$$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where $K_a^\dagger:K\to H$ is the adjoint
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]), which exists
uniquely in finite dimensions ([[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]).
The composition $K_a\circ X\circ K_a^\dagger$ maps $K$ to $K$, so the sum
defines an output endomorphism for each input endomorphism $X$. The index set
$A$ may be empty; its sum is then the zero map. Zero operators are allowed in
a nonempty family.

derivations.claim: If $\dim H=0$ or $\dim K=0$, the input or output operator space is zero, so $\Phi=0$ and the empty family is a Kraus representation. Assume both dimensions are positive and choose an ordered orthonormal basis $(f_\alpha)_{\alpha<m}$ of $K$ by [F3]. If $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)=0$, its $(i,\alpha),(j,\beta)$ product-basis entry is the $(\alpha,\beta)$ entry of $\Phi(E_{ij})$ by [L1], so every $\Phi(E_{ij})=0$. For each $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, the finite sum $\sum_{i,j<n}x_{ij}E_{ij}$ whose coordinate entries are those of $X$ agrees with $X$ on each $e_j$; [F4] therefore makes it equal to $X$. Thus $\Phi=0$ and the empty family works also in this case.

Suppose $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)\ne0$. Let $S=J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)^{1/2}$ be its non-negative square root from [F2]. By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(v_a)_{a<nm}$ of $S$ with eigenvalues $s_a\ge0$. Then $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)=S^2=\sum_{a:s_a>0}s_a^2v_av_a^\dagger$. For each $a$ with $s_a>0$, put $w_a=s_av_a$ and write $w_a=\sum_{i<n,\alpha<m}w_{a,i\alpha}e_i\otimes f_\alpha$. Define the linear map $K_a:H\to K$ on the basis by $K_ae_i=\sum_{\alpha<m}w_{a,i\alpha}f_\alpha$.

For every $i,j<n$ and $\alpha,\beta<m$, the $(i,\alpha),(j,\beta)$ entry of [L1] is $\sum_{a:s_a>0}w_{a,i\alpha}\overline{w_{a,j\beta}}$. The $(\alpha,\beta)$ entry of $\sum_aK_aE_{ij}K_a^\dagger$ is $\sum_a(K_a)_{\alpha i}\overline{(K_a)_{\beta j}}$, which is the same sum because $(K_a)_{\alpha i}=w_{a,i\alpha}$ by construction and [F6] gives the conjugate-transpose matrix of $K_a^\dagger$. Therefore $\Phi(E_{ij})=\sum_aK_aE_{ij}K_a^\dagger$ for every matrix unit.

Every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$ is the finite coordinate combination $\sum_{i,j<n}x_{ij}E_{ij}$ established in step 1.1. By linearity, step 2.1 therefore gives $\Phi(X)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^\dagger$ for every $X$. There are at most $nm=\dim(H)\dim(K)$ retained operators because the eigenbasis of $S$ has $nm$ elements; when $J=0$ the empty family was handled in step 1.1. This is a finite Kraus representation by [L2].

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is

definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$ of $H$, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. The following are
equivalent: $\Phi$ is completely positive; $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ is
non-negative; and $\Phi$ has a finite Kraus representation.

$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$

$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.
